problem: The bullet says a singular problem arises when 'p blows up at an end (Bessel at x = 0)'. For Bessel on (0, 1) the chapter itself gives p = x, so p vanishes at x = 0; it does not blow up. What blows up at x = 0 is q = −ν²/x. As written, this contradicts Section 3 and gives students the wrong picture of why Bessel is singular.
fix: Singular problem: p vanishes at an end (Legendre at x = ±1 where p = 1 − x² → 0; Bessel at x = 0 where p = x → 0), or q or w blows up at an end (Bessel: q = −ν²/x → ∞ as x → 0), or the interval is infinite.

where: Section 2, paragraph after the Lagrange identity
problem: The sign is flipped. Substituting L y = −λ w y into ∫(u L v − v L u) dx gives (λ_m − λ_n) ∫ w y_m y_n dx = 0, not (λ_n − λ_m) times the integral. The conclusion is unchanged because the right side is zero, but the step as printed is not the one the identity produces.
fix: Write (λ_m − λ_n) ∫_a^b w y_m y_n dx = 0, and since λ_m ≠ λ_n the integral must vanish.

problem: The regularity conditions omit w > 0 on [a, b], although the chapter insists on w > 0 earlier. Without w > 0 the weighted inner product and the norm √(∫ w y² dx) can fail.
fix: Regular problem: p > 0 on [a, b], p′ continuous, and q, w continuous on [a, b] with w > 0 there.

where: Section 2, 'the eigenvalues are simple and countable'
problem: Simplicity holds for a regular Sturm–Liouville problem with separated boundary conditions. With periodic boundary conditions the same λ can carry two independent eigenfunctions (for example sin nx and cos nx on [−π, π]), so the unqualified claim is too strong.
fix: For a regular problem with separated boundary conditions the eigenvalues are real, simple and countable, ordered λ₁ < λ₂ < λ₃ < … → ∞, with one eigenfunction each. Periodic conditions can give a repeated eigenvalue with two eigenfunctions.

where: Section 1, 'Any a(x) y″ + b(x) y′ + c(x) y = 0 reaches this form after one multiplication'
problem: The division by a(x) silently assumes a(x) ≠ 0 on the interval, and the reduction only works when λ enters c(x) linearly. Neither condition is stated.
fix: Any a(x) y″ + b(x) y′ + c(x) y = 0 with a(x) ≠ 0 on the interval, and with c(x) = c₀(x) + λ (λ entering linearly), reaches this form after dividing by a and multiplying by μ(x) = exp(∫ (b/a) dx).
